4.1.title: Therapeutic indications
4.1.text:
LYROKAUL is indicated in adults with primary hypercholesterolaemia (heterozygous familial (HeFH) and non-familial) or mixed dyslipidaemia as an adjunct to diet:
• in combination with a statin or statin with other lipid-lowering therapies in patients unable to reach low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) goals with the maximum tolerated dose of a statin, or
• alone or in combination with other lipid-lowering therapies in patients who are statin intolerant or for whom a statin is contraindicated.

4.2.title: Posology and method of administration
4.2.text:
Posology

The recommended dose is 300 mg administered as a single monthly subcutaneous injection.

The LDL-lowering effect of LYROKAUL may be measured between 25 - 31 days after initiation to assess response to treatment and, provided monthly dosing continued, anytime thereafter without regard to timing of the dose.

Missed doses

If a planned dose is missed by less than 7 days, LYROKAUL should be administered as soon as possible to maintain original dosing according to the patient’s monthly schedule.

If a planned dose is missed by 7 or more days, LYROKAUL should be administered as soon as possible and a new monthly schedule should be initiated based on this date.

Special populations

Elderly No dose adjustment is required for patients aged 65 years and above (see section 5.1).

Renal impairment No dose adjustment is required for patients with mild and moderate renal impairment. LYROKAUL has not been studied in patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease. (see sections 4.4, 5.2).

Hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is required for patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment. LYROKAUL has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease. (see sections 4.4, 5.2).

Paediatric population The safety and efficacy of LYROKAUL in children or adolescents aged under 18 years have not been established. No data are available.

Method of administration

For subcutaneous use only.

LYROKAUL is administered by subcutaneous injection into the abdomen; alternative injection sites include the upper front thighs. If injected by a healthcare professional or caregiver, the back of the upper arms can also be used as a site of injection. The injection site may be rotated if desired. Injections should not be given into areas of active skin disease or injury such as sunburns, skin rashes, inflammation or skin infections. Guidance should be provided by a healthcare professional on proper subcutaneous injection technique, prior to the patient or caregiver administering the product.

Each pre-filled syringe is for single use only. The plunger of the pre-filled syringe should be pushed down until the syringe is empty.

For instructions on the handling of the medicinal product before administration, see section 6.6.

Detailed instructions for use are provided at the end of the package leaflet.

4.3.title: Contraindications
4.3.text: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

4.4.title: Special warnings and precautions for use
4.4.text:
Traceability

In order to improve the traceability of biological medicinal products, the name and the batch number of the administered product should be clearly recorded.

Excipients with known effect

Sodium

This medicinal product contains less than 1 mmol sodium (23 mg) per dose, that is to say essentially ‘sodium-free’.

Polysorbate 80 This medicinal product contains 0.24 mg polysorbate 80 (E 433) per dose. Polysorbates may cause allergic reactions.

Renal impairment

LYROKAUL should be used with caution in patients with severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease. LYROKAUL has not been studied in these populations (see sections 4.2, 5.2).

Severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease

LYROKAUL has not been studied in patients with severe hepatic impairment or active liver disease. LYROKAUL should only be used in these patients if the anticipated clinical benefit outweighs the risk (see sections 4.2 and 5.2).

4.8.title: Undesirable effects
4.8.text:
Summary of the safety profile

The most frequently reported adverse reactions occurring in patients treated with lerodalcibep are injection site reaction (6.7%), injection site erythema (3.6%), and injection site bruising (1.6%).

Description of selected adverse reactions

Injection site reactions Injection site reactions occurred in 11.6% of patients treated with lerodalcibep in the pivotal studies. The most frequently occurring injection site reactions in patients treated with lerodalcibep were injection site reaction (6.7%), injection site erythema (3.6%), injection site pruritis (1.0 %) and injection site bruising (1.6%). The proportion of patients who discontinued treatment due to injection site reactions was 1.0%. Adverse reactions were generally mild or moderate in severity, 0.2 % injection site reactions were severe, transient, resolved and did not lead to discontinuation of study drug.

Immunogenicity Anti-drug antibody (ADA) responses, including neutralising antibodies (Nab), were low titer and did not appear to have a clinically meaningful impact on the efficacy or safety of lerodalcibep, except for a higher rate of injection site reactions in patients with treatment emergent ADA compared to patients who were ADA negative.

Reporting of suspected adverse reactions

Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.

5.1.title: Pharmacodynamic properties
5.1.text:
Pharmacotherapeutic group: Lipid modifying agents, other lipid modifying agents, ATC code: C10AX19

Mechanism of action

Lerodalcibep is a fusion protein that binds Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9). PCSK9 is a negative regulator of the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). PCSK9 binds to LDLR on the surface of hepatocytes to promote LDLR degradation within the liver. By inhibiting the binding of PCSK9 to LDLR, lerodalcibep prevents the degradation of the LDLR and increases its recycling and the number of LDLRs available to clear LDL from the blood, thereby lowering LDL-C levels.

Pharmacodynamic effects

After treatment with 300 mg lerodalcibep every month, strong (> 90%) suppression of PCSK9 is predicted to occur within 24 hours after subcutaneous administration and maintain throughout the 4- week dosing interval.

In the clinical studies, following monthly doses of lerodalcibep up to week 48, LDL-C, total cholesterol, ApoB, and non-HDL-C were reduced.

Cardiac electrophysiology In study 001 at a dose 2 times the maximum recommended dose, lerodalcibep does not prolong the QT intervals to any clinically relevant extent (n=5).

Clinical efficacy and safety

Following selection of dose and dosing frequency, lerodalcibep was evaluated in 3 large global randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies that enrolled 2 017 adults with HeFH, or clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), or very high or high risk for ASCVD, who were on stable diet and maximally tolerated statin therapy and who required additional LDL-C lowering. Demographics and baseline disease characteristics were balanced between the treatment arms in all studies.

In phase 3 studies, the average reduction in serum LDL-C throughout the dosing interval was 66.7%, and 73% of patients achieved a > 50% reduction in serum LDL-C throughout the dosing interval with 81.5% of patients a pre-dose steady-state serum LDL-C concentration < 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL).

The effect of lerodalcibep on cardiovascular morbidity and mortality has not yet been determined.

LDL-C reduction in adult patients with ASCVD, very high and high risk for ASCVD and HeFH LIB003-002 was a US multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 12-week study in which 81 patients with ASCVD, high risk for ASCVD and elevated LDL-C were randomised 1:1:1:1 to receive subcutaneous injections of either lerodalcibep 150 mg (n=21), lerodalcibep 300 mg (n=19), lerodalcibep 350 mg (n=21) or placebo (n=20) every 4 weeks (28 ± 3 days). Patients were on stable diet, and oral lipid lowering medicinal products (statin or other oral lipid modifying therapy), and LDL-C > 2.1 mmol/L (80 mg/dL) with CVD or ≥ 2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) without CVD.

The mean age at baseline was 65 years (range: 31 to 85 years), 54% aged above 65 years, 53% were women, 74% were White, 24% were Black, no patients identified as Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Forty eight percent (48%) patients had diabetes at baseline. The mean baseline LDL-C was 3.1 mmol/L (121 mg/dL). At the time of randomisation, 100% of patients were receiving statin therapy, and 46% were receiving high-intensity statin therapy.

The primary efficacy outcome measure in LIB003-002 was the placebo-adjusted percent change from baseline to week 12 in LDL-C. The difference between the lerodalcibep 300 mg and placebo groups in mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline to week 12 was - 77.3% (95% CI: - 90.5%, - 64.1%; p < 0.0001). LIB003-005 and LIB003-006 were both multicenter, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 52- week studies in which 1 844 adults with ASCVD, very high risk for ASCVD or high risk for ASCVD were randomised 2:1 to receive subcutaneous injections of either lerodalcibep 300 mg (n=1 229) or placebo (n=615) every 4 weeks. Patients were stable on diet, maximally tolerated dose of statin with or without other oral lipid modifying therapy and required additional LDL-C reduction.

The mean age in LIB003-005 at baseline was 64 years (range: 25 to 90 years), 49% aged above 65 years, 16% aged 75 years and above, 30% were women, 80% were White, 17% were Black, 3% were Asian and 1.1% identified as Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Thirty four percent (34%) of patients had diabetes at baseline, 86% clinical CVD and 14% at very high risk for CVD. The mean baseline LDL-C was 2.6 mmol/L (102 mg/dL). At the time of randomisation, 87% of patients were receiving statin therapy, with 54% of these patients receiving high-intensity statin therapy.

The primary efficacy outcome measures in LIB003-005 were the placebo adjusted ITT analysis of percent change from baseline to week 52 and the mean of weeks 50 and 52 in LDL-C. The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline to week 52 was - 55% (95% CI: - 59%, - 51%; p-value < 0.0001) and from baseline to the mean of weeks 50 and 52 was - 61% (95% CI: - 65, - 57). No attenuation of efficacy was seen during the 52-week treatment period. For additional results, see Table 3 and Figure 1.

Secondary efficacy outcome measures in LIB003-005 included the percent change from baseline to week 52 for total cholesterol (TC), non-HDL-cholesterol (non-HDL-C), and apolipoprotein B (ApoB). The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in TC from baseline to week 52 was - 31% (95% CI: - 33%, - 28%; p < 0.0001). The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in non-HDL-C from baseline to week 52 was - 45% (95% CI: - 48%, - 41%; p < 0.0001).The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in ApoB from baseline to week 52 was - 40% (95% CI: - 44%, - 37%; p-value < 0.0001).

LIB003-004 was a global multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 24-week study in which 478 patients with HeFH were randomised 2:1 to receive subcutaneous injections of either lerodalcibep 300 mg (n=319) or placebo (n=159) every 4 weeks. Patients were stable on diet, maximally tolerated dose of statin, with or without other oral lipid modifying therapy, and required additional LDL-C reduction.

The mean age at baseline was 53 years (range: 18 to 80 years), 19% aged above 65 years, 52% were women, 87% were White, 8% were Black, 5% were Asian and 1% identified as Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Ten percent (10%) of patients had diabetes at baseline. The mean baseline LDL-C was 3.9 mmol/L (150 mg/dL). At the time of randomisation, 89% of patients were receiving statin therapy with 67% receiving high-intensity doses, and 50% also on ezetimibe.

The primary efficacy outcome measure in LIB003-004 was the percent change from baseline to week 24 and the mean of weeks 22 and 24 in LDL-C. The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in LDL-C from baseline to week 24 was - 59% (95% CI: - 65%,
- 52%; p < 0.0001) and from baseline to the mean of weeks 20 and 22 - 65% (95% CI: - 71, - 59. No attenuation of efficacy was seen during the 24-week treatment period. For additional results, see Table 5 and Figure 3.

Secondary efficacy outcome measures in LIB003-004 included the percent change from baseline to week 24 for total cholesterol (TC), non-HDL-cholesterol (non-HDL-C), and apolipoprotein B (ApoB). The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in TC from baseline to week 24 was - 37% (95% CI: - 41%, - 32%; p < 0.0001). The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in non-HDL-C from baseline to week 24 was - 51% (95% CI: - 57%, - 45%; p < 0.0001). The difference between the lerodalcibep and placebo groups in mean percentage change in ApoB from baseline to week 24 was - 44% (95% CI: - 49%, - 39%; p < 0.0001).

Paediatric population

The European Medicines Agency has deferred the obligation to submit the results of studies with lerodalcibep in one or more subsets of the paediatric population in the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia (see section 4.2 for information on paediatric use).

5.2.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
5.2.text:
Absorption

Following a single subcutaneous administration, systemic exposure to lerodalcibep increased in a dose proportional manner over a range from 75 mg to 300 mg of lerodalcibep. The estimated subcutaneous bioavailability is 83%. Based on the population pharmacokinetic analysis, at the recommended dosing regimen of 300 mg of lerodalcibep, the estimated time to maximum serum concentration was 6 days (range 2-9 days) post-dose with a mean Cmax of 31.4 mcg/mL and mean AUCtau of 12 600 mcg*h/mL at steady state. Steady state was reached following 2-3 doses with approximately 30% increase in lerodalcibep serum concentrations.
